fields.title-post: Training in Institutional Food Service: What Will Actually Be Required in 2026
fields.rt-blog-html:
Between the Health Management Plan (PMS) that must be kept up to date, the EGalim law that is reshaping school menus, and the aggressive marketing tactics of organizations that exploit ambiguities in the regulations, it’s not always easy to tell fact from fiction.

To distinguish between misconceptions and genuine requirements, one question stands out: In 2026, who really needs training at your institution, in what areas, and under what conditions?

Whether you manage a school central kitchen, a corporate cafeteria, or a nursing home dining facility, the rules aren’t quite the same as those for traditional restaurants. Here’s a comprehensive guide to helping your teams comply with regulations, protect your guests, and approach inspections with peace of mind.

Why Training Is a Key Issue in Institutional Food Service

In the food service industry, food safety is a top priority for all professionals. But in institutional food service, even the smallest mistake immediately takes on a whole new scale. You prepare large quantities of food and serve meals daily to often vulnerable populations: young children in school cafeterias, hospital patients, or elderly residents in nursing homes. A simple break in the cold chain or an oversight during equipment cleaning can affect dozens, or even hundreds, of diners in a single meal service.

Beyond the legal requirement, training in institutional food service is your best line of defense. It protects the health of your guests, ensures the safety of your cooks and food service staff, and safeguards the reputation of your establishment or organization.

👉 See also: What are the different management models in institutional food service?

‍

Food Safety and HACCP: Regulatory Requirements for Institutional Food Service

Is hygiene training mandatory in institutional food service?

Yes, food safety training is required by law for all staff who handle food in institutional food service settings. However, contrary to a widespread misconception, institutional food service establishments are not required to complete the 14-hour HACCP training mandated by Decree 2011-731, which applies only to commercial food service.

This requirement stems from the European regulation (Hygiene Package), which mandates that employees possess the appropriate skills for each position, without specifying a single number of training hours or a specific accredited organization.

Commercial Food Service (restaurants, fast-food establishments, cafes)

  • Regulatory Framework: Decree 2011-731
  • Training requirement: 14 hours of mandatory training
  • Staff involved: At least 1 person per facility
  • Organization: ROFHYA-accredited organization (required)

Institutional Food Service (schools, healthcare facilities, businesses, nursing homes)

  • Regulatory Framework: Hygiene Package (Regulation (EC) No. 852/2004)
  • Training requirement: continuing education tailored to the job
  • Affected personnel: all food handlers
  • Organization: Valid internal or external training

The Hygiene Package and Decree 2011-731: Don't Confuse the Two Anymore

This is the most common misunderstanding during an inspection. Perhaps you’ve heard that your general manager is required to complete a 14-hour training course listed in the national registry? That’s not true.

European Regulation (EC) No. 852/2004 (the Hygiene Package) is the framework regulation that applies to institutional food service operations, whether directly managed or operated under a concession, in both the public and private sectors. It stipulates that operators must ensure that food handlers receive instructions and/or training in food hygiene appropriate to their professional activities.

French Decree No. 2011-731 requires the presence of at least one person who has completed the 14-hour HACCP training course through an organization listed in the ROFHYA registry. Its specifications are now set forth inthe order of February 12, 2024, whose title is unambiguous: it aims to provide training “tailored to the activities of commercial food service establishments.”

This interpretation is confirmed byTechnical Directive DGAL/SDSSA/2026-185 of April 3, 2026, which states that the national training requirement stems from the Agricultural Modernization Act No. 2010-874 (Article L233-4 of the Rural and Maritime Fisheries Code), established “for commercial food service activities.”

In other words: If an organization approaches you claiming that your central kitchen or company cafeteria must undergo a 14-hour ROFHYA training course, ask them what regulation they are basing this on. Keep these two references handy.

The Public Health Management Plan at the Heart of the System

Your Sanitation Control Plan (PMS) is a dynamic tool for ensuring food safety. During an audit or inspection by the DDPP (Departmental Directorate for Population Protection), the inspector will verify whether your HACCP procedures are understood and implemented on the ground.

Let’s take a concrete example: if your employees follow the vegetable processing plant’s cleaning plan or record the core temperature of test samples without understanding why they’re doing it, your system is vulnerable. Raising awareness of HACCP principles serves precisely to give meaning to these daily tasks: traceability, temperature management, vegetable decontamination, and prevention of cross-contamination.

👉 See also: The HACCP Approach in Institutional Food Service: The Complete Guide and The 12 Steps of the HACCP Method

Who needs training, and when?

  • Upon Hiring: Every new employee (permanent, contract, or temporary) must receive initial training before joining the production line or service team.
  • On an ongoing basis: Regular updates are required whenever a malfunction is detected (non-compliance during a routine inspection, discrepancies in temperature readings) or when new equipment or procedures are introduced.

What DDPP inspectors actually check

During a health inspection (Alim’confiance), the inspector doesn’t just check to see if a certificate is hanging on the wall. He or she will:

  • request the facility's hygiene training plan;
  • verify the certificates or attendance records for internal awareness-raising sessions;
  • Ask the kitchen staff direct questions to assess their actual on-the-job knowledge (how long it takes for a dish to cool, handling returns from the self-service line, etc.).

👉 See also: Health Inspections at Your Restaurant: Everything You Need to Know

‍

Other training courses to consider: allergens, nutrition, and prevention

In addition to microbiological safety, there are other requirements and recommendations that guide the professional development of your teams.

1. Allergen Management: A Strict Requirement

The European INCO Regulation (No. 1169/2011) requires that guests be informed of the presence of 14 allergens that must be declared: gluten, shellfish, eggs, peanuts, milk, tree nuts, etc.

  • In school and early childhood food services: Individualized Care Plans (PAI) require absolute precision. Your kitchen and service staff must be thoroughly trained to read product labels, follow technical specifications, and prevent cross-contamination during plating.
  • Whether in a business or in the healthcare sector: written information must be immediately accessible to guests, whether through a menu display, a digital kiosk, or an updated register.

2. Nutrition and the EGalim Act: Protein Diversification

Nutritional quality in institutional food service is strictly regulated by the decree of September 30, 2011, for schools, and further expanded by the EGalim Act.

The EGalim Act requires the implementation of a protein diversification plan, including a weekly vegetarian menu in school cafeterias. There is no legal requirement to hold a diploma or certificate to enroll in a “nutrition training program for institutional food service.”

However, in practice, training your chefs in plant-based culinary techniques (working with legumes, seasoning, nutritional balance) is the only way to ensure that your guests will find the menus appealing and to combat food waste.

3. Occupational Risk Prevention: Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) and the Occupational Risk Prevention Plan (PRAP)

Carrying heavy loads, working in a damp and slippery environment, and handling sharp tools: commercial kitchens pose real physical risks.

PRAP (Prevention of Risks Related to Physical Activity) training and first aid (SST – Workplace First Aid Responder) are strongly recommended. Even though the Labor Code imposes a general safety obligation on employers—rather than requiring specific PRAP training for everyone—investing in these modules directly reduces absenteeism and workplace accidents within your team.

Special Case: The Sale of Alcohol and the Operating License

This is a rare case, but it is worth clarifying: if you operate a food service facility (such as a company cafeteria, a military club, or a shelter) where alcoholic beverages are sold or served during special meals, the establishment must hold the appropriate license.

In this specific context, the department head must complete the 20-hour Operating Permit training course upon opening the facility (Article L3332-1-1 of the Public Health Code), which is generally spread over two and a half days. The permit is then valid for 10 years, and it is renewed by completing a refresher course of at least 6 hours.

👉 See also: How can you increase foot traffic at your restaurant in the institutional food service sector?

‍

Where can I get training? Organizations, costs, and funding

Once you’ve identified your needs, how should you go about it? Finding the right training center for institutional foodservice requires checking a few prerequisites.

Training Organizations: How to Choose?

You can choose from several types of actors:

  • The GRETA network: With a strong presence throughout the country, it is particularly well-suited for local governments and local government employees (CNFPT).
  • Specialized private organizations: hygiene consulting firms, engineering firms specializing in the agri-food industry and the foodservice sector.
  • In-house training: If you have a quality manager or an experienced general manager, you can design your own onboarding and awareness sessions. Simply document the materials and keep the sign-in sheets in your PMS.

Our advice: If you hire an external provider for a certification service, make sure they are Qualiopi-certified. This is a guarantee of quality and an essential requirement for receiving third-party funding.

Cost Ranges and Average Durations

Awareness of Basic Hygiene

  • Recommended format: in-house, short in-person session (half a day)
  • Estimated average cost: €0 if done in-house
  • Funding: Skills Development Plan

Advanced HACCP (14 hours)

  • Recommended format: external, in-house, or on-site (2 days)
  • Estimated average cost: €300 to €700 per trainee
  • Funding: OPCO or CNFPT

Plant-Based Cuisine and EGalim

  • Recommended format: hands-on in the kitchen, in-house (1 to 2 days)
  • Estimated average cost: €800 to €1,500 per group
  • Funding: OPCO or CNFPT

Funding Sources

  • No CPF for regulatory training: Following recent regulatory changes, training courses on strict hygiene or HACCP that are listed only in the specific registry are no longer eligible for the Personal Training Account (CPF). The employer is responsible for covering the costs.
  • For private institutions (whether under a management concession or directly managed by a private entity): contact your OPCO, specifically the OPCO Entreprises de Proximité (EP) or AKTO, depending on your industry. Partial or full funding is available under the skills development plan.
  • For the civil service (education, hospitals, local government): training programs are funded through the continuing education budgets for civil service employees—the CNFPT for local government and the ANFH for the hospital sector.

Training Certificate

At the end of each training session—whether external or internal—a single document must be issued and filed: the training certificate.

This document must include the exact title of the internship, its duration, the educational objectives, and the dates. Immediately file a copy in the employee’s personnel file and in the “Human Resources & Skills” section of your PMS. This is the first document the inspector will request in the event of an audit.

‍

The Importance of Reliable and Responsive Partners

Beyond theory, the success of a new kitchen organization depends on the quality of the support provided. Whether it’s training your teams or rolling out digital tools, surrounding yourself with reliable and responsive partners is essential to ensuring your teams are never left to fend for themselves on the job.

As a technology partner to hundreds of institutional food service establishments, Innovorder makes close collaboration a priority to help you modernize your operations with confidence. This support was praised by Ms. Sophie, an employee at an Inter-Administrative Restaurant (RIA), when she began using her Innovorder equipment:

“I received great support right from the start; everything went very smoothly. When I call support, they respond quickly. We resolve the issue right away. Support is responsive—just a call or an email, and it’s taken care of immediately.”

‍

FAQ — Training in Institutional Food Service

Is HACCP training required in school cafeterias?

Yes, training in food safety and HACCP principles is mandatory for all staff who handle food in school cafeterias, under the European Hygiene Package (Regulation (EC) No. 852/2004). However, unlike in the commercial food service industry, it is not mandatory to complete a specific 14-hour training course: appropriate and traceable awareness training as part of your Food Safety Management System (FSMS) is sufficient.

Who is required to undergo hygiene training in institutional food service?

All staff who handle food must receive training or be made aware of food safety practices: head chefs, cooks, kitchen assistants, as well as dining room staff, staff in the reheating station, and dishwashers. The training must be commensurate with the responsibilities and tasks actually performed by each employee.

How much does HACCP training cost?

On average, an external, inter-company training course costs between €300 and €700 per person for a full two-day module. If you choose to train your entire team on-site (in-house), prices range from €900 to €1,800 per training day for a group of 6 to 10 people.

Is there a legal validity period for the training?

No, the regulations do not mandate a strict expiration date, as is the case with the CACES or SST certifications. However, they do require ongoing refresher training. In practice, the DDPP inspection services recommend conducting a refresher course or training session on best practices every 3 to 5 years, or immediately following a major change in equipment or the identification of a health and safety non-compliance.

What is the difference between the HACCP method and the 14-hour hygiene training course?

HACCP is a method for analyzing hazards and controlling critical control points, applied on a daily basis in the kitchen. The 14-hour hygiene training course is a specific program mandated by French Decree 2011-731 exclusively for commercial food service establishments (traditional restaurants, fast-food restaurants). In institutional food service, proficiency in the HACCP method is mandatory, but completion of the 14-hour course offered by a ROFHYA-accredited center is not.

Give New Meaning to Your Training Plan

Training should never be viewed as just another item to check off an administrative list. When it’s designed with the field in mind, it becomes your teams’ greatest ally: stress-free, masterful techniques, DDPP inspections handled with confidence, and the assurance that you’re serving safe meals every day.

Why not take advantage of the next few days to assess your actual needs and give new meaning to your training plan?
